points.description: Explains why each removal needs more energy: removing an electron leaves fewer electrons, so electron-electron repulsion decreases, which lowers the potential energy of the remaining electrons. The student must state the decrease in repulsion and the decrease in potential energy.
points.partial_credit: 1 mark if only one of 'decreased electron-electron repulsion' or 'decreased potential energy' is stated, or if the link is missing.

points.description: Links potential energy to ionization energy: because the electron's potential energy is lower (more stable, more negative), more energy must be supplied to remove it, so ionization energy increases.
points.partial_credit: 1 mark if the link is stated but not explained, or if only the direction (higher IE) is given with no reason.

points.description: The 3rd and 4th electrons are removed from the n=3 shell and feel the same core charge, so they have the same radius and a similar attraction to the nucleus. Both facts must be stated.
points.partial_credit: 1 mark if only one of 'same core charge' or 'same n=3 shell / same radius' is stated.

points.description: The 5th electron is removed from the n=2 shell, which is closer to the nucleus. It feels a higher core charge and has a smaller radius, so the stronger Coulomb attraction explains the much larger jump to 16091 kJ/mol. Both the higher core charge and the smaller radius must be stated.
points.partial_credit: 1 mark if only one of 'higher core charge' or 'smaller radius / n=2 shell' is stated, or if the jump is noted without the reason.

rubric.notes: Full marks need the repulsion-to-potential-energy-to-ionization-energy chain (P1 and P2), the same core charge and radius for the 3rd and 4th electrons from n=3 (P3), and the higher core charge and smaller radius for the 5th electron from n=2, which explains the large jump in energy (P4). Each point is all-or-nothing except for the half marks listed, which apply when only one of its two claims is stated or when the cause-and-effect link is missing. Restating the question, giving a general definition of ionization energy, or listing the values without a reason earns nothing.
